title: Greetings come in pairs
summary: Most Arabic greetings have a fixed reply. Learn them as pairs.
formula: greeting → fixed reply
explanation: When someone says السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (peace be upon you), the reply is وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ (and upon you be peace). صَبَاحُ الْخَيْر (morning of goodness) is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّور (morning of light). مَرْحَبًا (hello) is often answered with مَرْحَبًا or أَهْلًا. These are fixed phrases: say them exactly, even if you don't analyse every word yet.

head: Greeting
Reply
Meaning
rows: peace be upon you / and upon you be peace

examples.en: Good morning, Sami!
Good morning (reply), Layla!

title: I, you, he, she
summary: Arabic has a different word for 'you' when you speak to a man and to a woman.
formula: أَنَا I · أَنْتَ you (m) · أَنْتِ you (f) · هُوَ he · هِيَ she
explanation: The words look almost the same on paper: only the last vowel changes. أَنْتَ (anta) is for a man, أَنْتِ (anti) for a woman. Without harakat both are written أنت, so the vowel marks matter while you learn.

examples.en: I am Sami.
She is Layla.

title: my, your: endings on the noun
summary: 'My' and 'your' are endings joined to the end of the noun.
formula: noun + ـِي (my) · ـُكَ (your, m) · ـُكِ (your, f)
explanation: اِسْم means 'name'. Add ـِي to get اِسْمِي (my name). Add ـُكَ when you talk to a man (اِسْمُكَ, your name) and ـُكِ when you talk to a woman (اِسْمُكِ). The ending is written joined to the word: never as a separate word.

examples.en: What is your name? (to a man)
My name is Layla.

title: No word for 'am / is / are'
summary: In the present tense, Arabic puts two words side by side without a verb 'to be'.
formula: subject + description  (أَنَا + مِصْرِيّ = I am Egyptian)
explanation: أَنَا مِصْرِيّ is literally 'I Egyptian'. The 'am' is understood. This kind of sentence, which starts with a noun or pronoun, is called a nominal sentence. Questions work the same way: أَيْنَ الْبَيْت؟ 'where (is) the house?'.

examples.en: I am from Egypt.
She is from Lebanon.

title: Nationality words: -ī and -iyya
summary: Add ـِيّ to a country to say a man's nationality, and ـِيَّة for a woman's.
formula: country + ـِيّ (m) · + ـِيَّة (f)
explanation: مِصْر (Egypt) → مِصْرِيّ (an Egyptian man) → مِصْرِيَّة (an Egyptian woman). Drop a final ā or the article first: لُبْنَان → لُبْنَانِيّ. The feminine adds ة, which you will meet on every feminine word.

examples.en: I am American. (man)
She is Lebanese.

title: Question words
summary: Question words go at the start of the sentence.
formula: question word + rest of the sentence + ؟
explanation: كَيْفَ (how), أَيْنَ (where), مَا (what, before a noun) and مَنْ (who) start the question. The Arabic question mark ؟ is a mirrored ?. For yes/no questions, put هَلْ at the start: هَلْ أَنْتَ مِصْرِيّ؟ (Are you Egyptian?).

examples.en: How are you? (to a woman)
Who is this?

title: this: هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ (gender)
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine. Use هٰذَا for masculine and هٰذِهِ for feminine.
formula: هٰذَا + masculine noun · هٰذِهِ + feminine noun
explanation: Most feminine nouns end in ة (a tied t): عَائِلَة, سَيَّارَة. Female people are feminine too, with or without ة: أُمّ (mother), بِنْت (girl). Note the small upright alif in هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ: it is a long ā that is not written as a full letter.

head: Masculine
Feminine
English
rows: this is a father / this is a mother
this is a brother / this is a sister
this is a book / this is a car

examples.en: This is my brother.
This is my mother.

title: the: الـ (al-)
summary: 'The' is الـ joined to the front of the noun. There is no word for 'a'.
formula: الـ + noun  (كِتَاب a book → الْكِتَاب the book)
explanation: A noun without الـ means 'a': كِتَاب = a book. With الـ it means 'the'. Before a sun letter the l is not said and the next letter is doubled (السَّيَّارَة as-sayyāra). Before a moon letter the l is said (الْقَلَم al-qalam).

examples.en: The book is new.
The car is big.

title: Adjectives follow and agree
summary: An adjective comes after its noun and matches it in gender and in 'the'.
formula: noun + adjective (same gender, both with or both without الـ)
explanation: كِتَاب جَدِيد = a new book. سَيَّارَة جَدِيدَة = a new car (feminine adds ة to the adjective). الْكِتَاب الْجَدِيد = the new book. But الْكِتَاب جَدِيد (only the noun has الـ) is a sentence: the book is new.

examples.en: I have a new pen.
The big bag is mine.

title: Numbers 1–10
summary: Learn the counting forms 1–10 and the Arabic digits ١ to ١٠.
formula: ١ وَاحِد · ٢ اِثْنَان · ٣ ثَلَاثَة … ١٠ عَشَرَة
explanation: These are the forms used when counting and in phone numbers. Arabic digits are written left to right inside right-to-left text: ١٢ is twelve. With nouns, 3–10 have special rules that come later in the course.

examples.en: My number is five seven three.
I have three brothers.

title: Jobs for men and women
summary: A job word for a woman usually adds ة to the word for a man.
formula: مُدَرِّس (m) + ة → مُدَرِّسَة (f)
explanation: طَالِب is a male student and طَالِبَة a female student. Almost every job works the same way: مُهَنْدِس → مُهَنْدِسَة, طَبِيب → طَبِيبَة. Use the form that matches the person: هِيَ طَبِيبَة (she is a doctor). There is no word for 'a': أَنَا مُمَرِّض means 'I am a nurse'. To ask about a job, say مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ to a man and مَا عَمَلُكِ؟ to a woman.

examples.en: My father is an engineer.
My mother is a doctor.

title: Noun + noun: 'the … of …' (iḍāfa)
summary: Put two nouns side by side to say 'the X of Y': يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَة, Friday (literally 'the day of Friday').
formula: noun (no الـ) + noun with الـ, a name or a 'my/your' ending
explanation: In كِتَابُ دَانْيَال (Daniel's book) the first noun never takes الـ, yet it is definite: 'the book of Daniel'. The second noun is a name, a noun with الـ, or a noun with an ending such as ـِي. A ة at the end of the first noun is said as t: مَدْرَسَةُ اللُّغَة (madrasatu l-lugha, the language school). In careful speech the first noun carries a case vowel (often -u) and the second takes -i; at the end of a sentence the last vowel is usually dropped.

examples.en: Today is Sunday.
This is Daniel's book.

title: Telling the time
summary: Say السَّاعَة (the hour) and a feminine ordinal: السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة, three o'clock.
formula: السَّاعَة + ordinal (f) + وَالرُّبْع / وَالنِّصْف / إِلَّا رُبْعًا
explanation: Ask كَمِ السَّاعَة؟ (what time is it?, literally 'how much is the hour?'). Answer with السَّاعَة and the feminine 'first, second, third…' word, because سَاعَة is feminine: السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة (five o'clock). One o'clock is السَّاعَة الْوَاحِدَة. Add وَالرُّبْع (and a quarter), وَالنِّصْف (and a half) or إِلَّا رُبْعًا (minus a quarter). Add صَبَاحًا for the morning and مَسَاءً for the evening. 'At' a time is فِي: فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة (at nine o'clock).

examples.en: What time is it now?
It is half past ten.

title: The present tense: I, you, he, she
summary: A present-tense verb adds a prefix for the person: a- for I, ta- for you, ya- for he.
formula: a- (I) · ta- (you, m) · ta- … -īna (you, f) · ya- (he) · ta- (she) + stem + -u
explanation: Arabic verbs change at the front to show who is doing the action. Take ذَهَبَ (he went): أَذْهَبُ (I go), تَذْهَبُ (you go, to a man), تَذْهَبِينَ (you go, to a woman), يَذْهَبُ (he goes), تَذْهَبُ (she goes). 'You' (m) and 'she' look the same; the pronoun or the context tells them apart. The pronoun is usually left out, because the verb already shows the person: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة means 'I go to school'. One present form covers 'I go', 'I am going' and 'I do go'.

examples.en: I wake up early.
She drinks tea.

title: We, you all, they: plural verbs
summary: With 'we' the prefix is na-; with 'you' (a group) and 'they' the verb also ends in -ūna.
formula: نَحْنُ نَدْرُسُ · أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ · هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ
explanation: You already know أَدْرُسُ (I study) and يَدْرُسُ (he studies). For 'we', the prefix is na-: نَدْرُسُ (we study). For 'you' talking to a group, and for 'they', the verb takes a prefix and the ending ـُونَ: أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ (you study), هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ (they study). أَنْتُمْ and هُمْ are used for groups of men and for mixed groups.

examples.en: We study Arabic.
They work at a company.

title: Not: لَا before a present verb
summary: Put لَا before a present-tense verb to say 'not': لَا أَعْرِفُ, I don't know.
formula: لَا + present verb
explanation: On its own لَا means 'no'. Before a present-tense verb it means 'not', and the verb itself does not change: أَفْهَمُ (I understand) → لَا أَفْهَمُ (I don't understand); يَعْمَلُ (he works) → لَا يَعْمَلُ (he doesn't work). English needs 'do' or 'does'; Arabic does not. لَا is only for verbs: to say 'I am not …' in a sentence without a verb, Arabic uses لَيْسَ, which comes in week 5.

examples.en: I don't know.
I don't understand this word.

title: Colours: masculine and feminine
summary: The basic colours have a masculine form like أَحْمَر and a feminine form like حَمْرَاء.
formula: m: aCCaC (أَحْمَر) · f: CaCCāʾ (حَمْرَاء)
explanation: The basic colours share one pattern. The masculine starts with أَ: أَحْمَر (red), أَزْرَق (blue). The feminine has a different shape ending in ـَاء: حَمْرَاء, زَرْقَاء. Like every adjective, a colour comes after its noun and matches it: قَلَم أَحْمَر (a red pen), سَيَّارَة حَمْرَاء (a red car). Some colours come from things and work like nationality words, with ـِيّ and ـِيَّة: بُنِّيّ, بُنِّيَّة (brown, from coffee beans).

examples.en: The pen is red.
The car is white.

title: The object ending -an
summary: The object of a verb takes the ending -a: -an (tanwīn) without 'the', a single -a with الـ.
formula: verb + object: آكُلُ خُبْزًا (I eat bread) · أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ (I drink tea)
explanation: In آكُلُ خُبْزًا (I eat bread), خُبْز is the object, the thing that is eaten, so it ends in -an. This ending is written as two fathas, usually with an extra alif: خُبْزًا, شَايًا. After ة there is no extra alif: قَهْوَةً. A word with الـ never has tanwīn, so a definite object ends in a single fatha: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ. Arabic uses الـ for things in general, where English uses no article at all. In everyday speech, and at the end of a sentence, the ending is often not pronounced, but you will see it in careful writing.

examples.en: I eat bread and cheese for breakfast.
Do you drink tea or coffee? (to a woman)

title: Ordering politely: أُرِيدُ … مِنْ فَضْلِكَ
summary: Order with أُرِيدُ (I'd like) + the thing you want + 'please'. Ask what there is with هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ…؟
formula: أُرِيدُ + object (-an) + مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ
explanation: أُرِيدُ means 'I want', and with 'please' it is the normal polite way to order: أُرِيدُ شَايًا، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (I'd like a tea, please). 'Please' changes with the person you speak to: مِنْ فَضْلِكَ to a man, مِنْ فَضْلِكِ to a woman. لَوْ سَمَحْتَ / لَوْ سَمَحْتِ ('if you allow') is just as polite and is also how you catch a waiter's attention. To ask what a café has, say هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ…؟ (do you have…?). A cup or a bottle comes first, then the drink: فِنْجَانُ قَهْوَة (a cup of coffee), زُجَاجَةُ مَاء (a bottle of water). After أُرِيدُ the first word takes the object ending: أُرِيدُ فِنْجَانَ قَهْوَة.

examples.en: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

examples.ar: أُرِيدُ شَايًا بِدُونِ سُكَّر، لَوْ سَمَحْتِ.
examples.en: I'd like a tea without sugar, please. (to a woman)

title: Sound plurals: -ūna and -āt
summary: Add ـُونَ for a group of men or a mixed group, and ـَات for women and many things. The singular stays whole.
formula: طَبَّاخ → طَبَّاخُونَ (-ūna) · سَلَطَة → سَلَطَات (-āt)
explanation: The masculine sound plural adds ـُونَ: طَبَّاخ (cook) → طَبَّاخُونَ (cooks), مِصْرِيّ → مِصْرِيُّونَ (Egyptians). After a verb or a preposition the ending becomes ـِينَ: شُكْرًا لِلطَّبَّاخِينَ (thanks to the cooks). It is used for people, and adjectives that describe male people take it too: طَبَّاخُونَ مُمْتَازُونَ. The feminine sound plural drops ة and adds ـَات: سَلَطَة → سَلَطَات, طَبَّاخَة → طَبَّاخَات. Many masculine words for things also take ـَات: مَشْرُوب → مَشْرُوبَات (drinks). Important: the plural of a thing takes a feminine singular adjective: مَشْرُوبَات بَارِدَة (cold drinks), سَلَطَات كَثِيرَة (many salads).

Plural
Rule
rows: after a verb or preposition: + ـِينَ

examples.en: The cooks in this restaurant are Egyptian.
We have salads and cold drinks.

title: Likes and dislikes: أُحِبُّ and يُعْجِبُنِي
summary: أُحِبُّ + الـ noun = I like (things in general take الـ). لَا أُحِبُّ = I don't like. With يُعْجِبُنِي the thing you like is the subject.
formula: (لَا) أُحِبُّ + الـ noun (-a) · يُعْجِبُنِي / تُعْجِبُنِي + الـ noun
explanation: أُحِبُّ means 'I like' and 'I love'. Something you like in general takes الـ, and as the object it ends in -a: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ (I like coffee). For 'I don't like', put لَا directly before the verb: لَا أُحِبُّ الطَّعَامَ الْحَارَّ. To make it stronger, add كَثِيرًا (a lot) or, with a negative, أَبَدًا (at all). The verb changes with the person: أُحِبُّ (I), تُحِبُّ (you, to a man), تُحِبِّينَ (you, to a woman), يُحِبُّ (he), نُحِبُّ (we). A second way is يُعْجِبُنِي, literally 'it pleases me'. Here the food is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: يُعْجِبُنِي الْكُشَرِي (masculine), تُعْجِبُنِي الْقَهْوَة (feminine).

examples.en: I like coffee a lot.
I don't like spicy food.

title: Broken plurals
summary: Most plurals change the vowels inside the word: كِتَاب → كُتُب, صَحْن → صُحُون. Plurals of things take a feminine singular adjective.
formula: same root letters, new vowel pattern: صَحْن → صُحُون · قَلَم → أَقْلَام
explanation: The root letters stay, but the vowels around them change: كِتَاب (book) → كُتُب, صَحْن (plate) → صُحُون, قَلَم (pen) → أَقْلَام, مِلْعَقَة (spoon) → مَلَاعِق. Some patterns are common (aCCāC, CuCūC, maCāCiC), but you cannot always guess the plural, so learn each noun with its plural. Two rules of agreement: (1) a plural of things counts as feminine singular, so it takes an adjective with ة and the pronoun هِيَ: الصُّحُون كَبِيرَة، هِيَ فِي الْمَطْبَخ. (2) A plural of people takes a plural adjective: أَصْدِقَاء كَثِيرُونَ (many friends). After the numbers three to ten the noun is plural: عَشَرَة أَرْغِفَة (ten loaves).

examples.en: These are new books.
Where are the spoons? They are in the kitchen.

title: The dual: exactly two
summary: For two of something add ـَانِ (subject, on its own) or ـَيْنِ (after a verb or preposition). ة becomes ت.
formula: كُوب → كُوبَانِ / كُوبَيْنِ · شَطِيرَة → شَطِيرَتَانِ / شَطِيرَتَيْنِ
explanation: Arabic has a special form for exactly two things or people, the dual. Add ـَانِ to the singular: كِتَاب → كِتَابَانِ (two books). After a verb or a preposition the ending is ـَيْنِ: أُرِيدُ كُوبَيْنِ (I'd like two glasses), مِنْ بَلَدَيْنِ (from two countries). A feminine ة is written as an open ت before the ending, and you hear the t: شَطِيرَة → شَطِيرَتَانِ. The dual already means 'two', so you normally don't add the number; اِثْنَانِ (m) or اِثْنَتَانِ (f) after the noun only adds emphasis. Adjectives agree and take the same ending: الْكُوبَانِ كَبِيرَانِ (the two glasses are big). To say 'two glasses of juice', use مِنْ: كُوبَانِ مِنَ الْعَصِير.

examples.en: I have two books.
I'd like two sandwiches, please.

title: Numbers 11–100 and prices
summary: 11–19 are two words (خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ), the tens end in ـُونَ (ثَلَاثُونَ), and 21–99 are 'five and twenty'. After 11–99 the noun is singular with -an: عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا.
formula: ١٥ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ · ٢٠ عِشْرُون · ٧٥ خَمْسَة وَسَبْعُونَ · ١٠٠ مِئَة
explanation: 11 is أَحَدَ عَشَرَ and 12 is اِثْنَا عَشَرَ. 13 to 19 are 'three-ten' to 'nine-ten': ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ, خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ. The tens add ـُونَ: عِشْرُون (20, the odd one out), ثَلَاثُون, أَرْبَعُون, خَمْسُون, سِتُّون, سَبْعُون, ثَمَانُون, تِسْعُون. Like the sound plural, they end in ـِينَ after a verb or a preposition: بِعِشْرِينَ (for twenty). From 21 to 99 the unit comes first, joined by وَ: خَمْسَة وَسَبْعُونَ is 'five and seventy', 75. 100 is مِئَة. The counted noun changes with the number: after 3–10 it is plural (ثَلَاثَة جُنَيْهَات), after 11–99 it is singular with the ending -an (عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا), and after مِئَة it is singular (مِئَةُ جُنَيْه). These forms are for a masculine noun such as جُنَيْه; with feminine nouns some units change, which comes later in the course. To ask a price, say بِكَمْ؟ (for how much?).

examples.en: It's twenty pounds a kilo.
The total is seventy-five pounds.

title: Verb first: the verbal sentence
summary: A sentence that starts with a verb is a verbal sentence. Before its subject the verb stays singular, even when the subject is plural.
formula: verb + subject (+ object)  (يَزُورُ السُّيَّاحُ الْمَتْحَفَ = the tourists visit the museum)
explanation: Arabic often puts the verb first: يَذْهَبُ سَامِي إِلَى الْمَسْجِد (Sami goes to the mosque). The verb shows the gender of the subject: يَـ for a man or a masculine noun, تَـ for a woman or a feminine noun, as in تَذْهَبُ لَيْلَى (Layla goes). When the verb comes first it stays singular, even with a plural subject: يَزُورُ السُّيَّاحُ الْمَتْحَفَ, never يَزُورُونَ السُّيَّاحُ. In careful Arabic the subject ends in -u and the object in -a (as-suyyāḥu, al-matḥafa), but these endings are usually dropped at the end of a sentence.

examples.en: The tourists visit the museum every day.
Layla goes to the bookshop.

title: First, second, third: ordinal numbers
summary: Ordinals are adjectives: they come after the noun and agree with it in gender and in 'the'.
formula: noun + ordinal  (الشَّارِع الثَّانِي the second street · الْبِنَايَة الثَّالِثَة the third building)
explanation: Apart from أَوَّل (first), the ordinals are built from the numbers on the pattern fāʿil: ثَلَاثَة (three) → الثَّالِث (the third), خَمْسَة (five) → الْخَامِس (the fifth). Like any adjective they follow the noun, take الـ when the noun has it, and add ة for a feminine noun: الْبِنَايَة الثَّالِثَة. The feminine of أَوَّل is irregular: الْأُولَى. أَوَّل can also stand in front of an indefinite noun: أَوَّلُ يَوْم (the first day).

examples.en: Take the second street on the right.
The bookshop is in the third building.

title: By bus, by taxi: bi-
summary: To say how you travel, join بِـ (by) to the vehicle with الـ. On foot is مَشْيًا.
formula: بِـ + الـ + vehicle  (بِالْمِتْرُو = by metro)
explanation: بِـ is a one-letter preposition, written joined to the next word. With the article it becomes bi-l-: بِالْحَافِلَة (by bus), بِالتَّاكْسِي (by taxi), بِالسَّيَّارَة (by car). The alif of الـ is still written but not said. For 'on foot' Arabic uses one word, مَشْيًا (walking). To take or ride a vehicle is يَرْكَبُ, with the vehicle straight after it and no preposition: يَرْكَبُ الطُّلَّابُ الْحَافِلَةَ (the students take the bus).

examples.en: I go to school by metro.
The students take the bus every morning.

title: Where things are: words of place
summary: Words like أَمَامَ (in front of) and خَلْفَ (behind) come straight before a noun, and that noun takes the ending -i.
formula: word of place + noun ending in -i  (خَلْفَ الْبَنْكِ = behind the bank)
explanation: Most words of place end in -a: أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, فَوْقَ, تَحْتَ, بَيْنَ, مُقَابِلَ. The noun after them is in the genitive case, so it ends in -i: أَمَامَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ (in front of the school). In speech this -i is often dropped at the end of a sentence. With a pronoun ending they work like nouns: خَلْفَهُ (behind it), خَلْفَكَ (behind you). Don't confuse فِي (in, inside) with عَلَى (on top of).

examples.en: The post office is behind the bank.
The book is on the table.

title: There is, there are: hunāka
summary: Put هُنَاكَ before an indefinite noun to say 'there is' or 'there are'. Add هَلْ in front to ask.
formula: هُنَاكَ + noun without الـ  (هُنَاكَ صَيْدَلِيَّة = there is a pharmacy)
explanation: هُنَاكَ literally means 'there'. At the start of a sentence it introduces something new: هُنَاكَ بَنْك فِي هٰذَا الشَّارِع (there is a bank on this street). The same word works for one thing or many: هُنَاكَ مَحَلَّات كَثِيرَة (there are many shops). To ask, put هَلْ in front: هَلْ هُنَاكَ صَيْدَلِيَّة قَرِيبَة؟ (is there a pharmacy nearby?). For 'there isn't', say لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ. You can also start with the place: فِي الْمَدِينَة مَسَاجِد كَثِيرَة (in the city there are many mosques). Don't mix up هُنَاكَ (there) and هُنَا (here).

examples.en: There is a pharmacy near here.

examples.ar: هَلْ هُنَاكَ بَنْك فِي هٰذَا الشَّارِع؟
examples.en: Is there a bank on this street?

title: Plurals of things count as 'she'
summary: The plural of a thing or an animal is treated as feminine singular: it takes هٰذِهِ, هِيَ and an adjective with ة.
formula: plural of things + feminine singular adjective  (الْقُمْصَان جَمِيلَة = the shirts are beautiful)
explanation: Arabic sorts plurals into two groups. Plurals of people keep a plural adjective: الْبَاعَة لُطَفَاء (the sellers are kind). But the plural of anything that is not a person, such as shirts, streets, shops or lanterns, behaves like one feminine word: الشَّوَارِع مُزْدَحِمَة (the streets are crowded), هٰذِهِ الْأَحْذِيَة غَالِيَة (these shoes are expensive). You also refer to them with هِيَ (she, it), and a verb takes the feminine تَـ.

examples.en: These shirts are very nice.
The shops are open until ten.

title: There is…: put the place first
summary: To say what there is somewhere, start with the place: فِي الشَّقَّة شُرْفَة (there is a balcony in the flat).
formula: فِي + place + thing (no الـ)
explanation: Arabic needs no word for 'there is'. Put the place first and the thing after it, without الـ: فِي الشَّقَّة مَطْبَخ (in the flat, a kitchen = there is a kitchen in the flat). To ask, put هَلْ in front: هَلْ فِي الشَّقَّة شُرْفَة؟ If the thing has الـ, use the normal order instead: الْمَطْبَخ فِي الشَّقَّة (the kitchen is in the flat). Instead of naming the place again, use فِيهِ (in it, masculine) or فِيهَا (in it, feminine): الشَّقَّة صَغِيرَة، وَفِيهَا شُرْفَة.

examples.en: There is a bedroom and a kitchen in the flat.
There is a big window in the living room.

title: All the possessive endings
summary: Eight endings say whose something is: my, your (to a man, a woman, several people), his, her, our and their.
formula: noun + ـِي · ـُكَ · ـُكِ · ـُهُ · ـُهَا · ـُنَا · ـُكُمْ · ـُهُمْ
explanation: You already know ـِي (my), ـُكَ and ـُكِ (your), ـُهُ (his) and ـُهَا (her). Add ـُنَا (our), ـُكُمْ (your, to several people) and ـُهُمْ (their). Before any ending, ة turns into ت: غُرْفَة → غُرْفَتِي, غُرْفَتُنَا. After an i sound, ـُهُ and ـُهُمْ become ـِهِ and ـِهِمْ: لِعَائِلَتِهِ (for his family). A noun with an ending is already definite, so it never takes الـ as well. The same endings go on little words like عِنْدَ, مَعَ and فِي: عِنْدَهُ (he has), مَعَنَا (with us), فِيهَا (in it).

examples.en: This is my room, and this is my bed.
Their house is in Chicago.

title: To have: عِنْدَ, لِـ and مَعَ
summary: Arabic has no verb 'to have'. It says 'at me', 'for me' or 'with me', using a possessive ending.
formula: عِنْدِي / لِي / مَعِي + thing (no الـ)
explanation: عِنْدِي سَيَّارَة is literally 'at me (is) a car', and it is the everyday way to say 'I have a car'. لِي (for me) is used above all for family and for what belongs to you: لِي أَخ وَأُخْت (I have a brother and a sister). مَعِي (with me) means you have something on you right now: مَعِي هَاتِفِي (I have my phone on me). Before an ending لِـ becomes لَـ: لَكَ, لَهُ, لَهَا, but لِي. To say you don't have something, put لَيْسَ in front: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي تِلْفَاز (I don't have a television).

examples.en: I have a new key for the flat.
I don't have a television.

title: Adjectives agree with their noun
summary: An adjective matches its noun in gender and in definiteness. A noun with an ending such as ـُهُ counts as definite.
formula: شَعْرُهُ الطَّوِيل = his long hair · شَعْرُهُ طَوِيل = his hair is long
explanation: On day 6 you met كِتَاب جَدِيد (a new book) and الْكِتَاب الْجَدِيد (the new book). A noun with a possessive ending is definite too, so an adjective that describes it takes الـ: شَعْرُهُ الطَّوِيل (his long hair). Without الـ the adjective says something about the noun, and you have a sentence: شَعْرُهُ طَوِيل (his hair is long). The adjective follows the gender of the noun, not of the owner: شَعْرُهَا طَوِيل (her hair is long), because شَعْر is masculine. For a group of people the adjective is plural: أَقَارِب كَثِيرُونَ (many relatives).

examples.en: Her hair is blond and long.
My little sister is very pretty.

title: is not: لَيْسَ
summary: لَيْسَ means 'is not'. It changes with the person, and the adjective after it ends in ـًا.
formula: لَيْسَ + adjective + ـًا  (هُوَ لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا)
explanation: Present-tense sentences have no word for 'is', but the negative does: لَيْسَ. It changes with the person like a verb: لَسْتُ (I am not), لَسْتَ and لَسْتِ (you are not), لَيْسَ (he is not), لَيْسَتْ (she is not), لَسْنَا (we are not). The adjective after it takes the accusative ending ـًا: هُوَ لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا. After ة the ending is ـَةً: هِيَ لَيْسَتْ طَوِيلَةً. In everyday speech this ending is often dropped, but write it. لَيْسَ also makes عِنْدِي negative: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَة.

examples.en: Omar is not tall; he is short.
Nour is not tall.

title: Saying your age
summary: Ask كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟ and answer عُمْرِي + number + years. The word for 'years' depends on the number.
explanation: عُمْر means 'age' (and 'life'). Add an ending: عُمْرِي (my age), عُمْرُكَ, عُمْرُكِ, عُمْرُهُ, عُمْرُهَا. To ask, use كَمْ (how much): كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟ After 3 to 10 comes the plural سَنَوَات, and because سَنَة is feminine the number loses its ة: عَشْرُ سَنَوَاتٍ (ten years), not عَشَرَة. From 11 upwards the singular follows, with the ending ـَةً: عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً. The round tens are easy: عِشْرُون, ثَلَاثُون, أَرْبَعُون, خَمْسُون, سِتُّون, سَبْعُون.

examples.en: How old are you, Daniel?
I am twenty years old.

title: Family chains: اِبْنُ عَمِّي
summary: Put two family words side by side to say 'the son of my uncle'. Only the last word takes 'my' or الـ.
formula: first word (no الـ, ending ـُ) + second word + ending  (اِبْنُ عَمِّي)
explanation: Arabic links two nouns to say 'X of Y' with no word for 'of': اِبْنُ عَمِّي = son (of) my uncle = my cousin. The first word never takes الـ or a possessive ending, and its last vowel is usually ـُ. 'My' goes on the last word only: زَوْجَةُ خَالِي (my uncle's wife). The last word can also be a name: خَالَةُ سَامِي (Sami's aunt). When the first word ends in ة, it is said as t: زَوْجَةُ (zawjatu). Note that أَخ (brother) and أَب (father) become أَخُو and أَبُو before another word: أَخُو أَبِي (my father's brother).

examples.en: Khalid is my cousin (my mother's sister's son).
My uncle's wife is Lebanese.

title: The past tense: I went, he went
summary: A past-tense verb adds an ending for each person: ذَهَبْتُ (I went), ذَهَبَ (he went), ذَهَبَتْ (she went).
formula: stem ذَهَب + ending: -tu (I) · -ta (you, m) · -ti (you, f) · -a (he) · -at (she) · -nā (we) · -tum (you, pl) · -ū (they)
explanation: The past tense is the simplest verb form, and it is the form dictionaries list: ذَهَبَ means 'he went', and it also names the verb 'to go'. To show who did the action, add an ending to the stem: ذَهَبْتُ (I went), ذَهَبَتْ (she went), ذَهَبْنَا (we went). The ending already shows the person, so the pronoun is usually left out: ذَهَبْتُ is enough for 'I went'. The verb often comes first in the sentence: ذَهَبَ سَامِي إِلَى الْبَحْر (Sami went to the sea). Watch the sukūn: ذَهَبْتُ (I went) and ذَهَبَتْ (she went) differ only in where the vowel is.

examples.en: Yesterday I went to Alexandria.
Sami came back by train in the evening.
We ate fish near the sea.

title: Didn't: مَا + past verb
summary: Put مَا before a past verb to say that something did not happen: مَا ذَهَبْتُ (I didn't go).
formula: مَا + past verb (the verb does not change)
explanation: مَا + a past verb is the quick, everyday way to say 'didn't': مَا فَعَلْتُ شَيْئًا (I didn't do anything). Nothing else changes: the verb keeps its normal past ending. You already know مَا as 'what' (مَا اسْمُكَ؟). Look at what follows it: in a statement, مَا directly before a past verb means 'not'. To ask 'what did you do?' Arabic uses مَاذَا: مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟ In formal writing لَمْ + the present form is preferred (day 41); it means the same.

examples.en: I didn't do anything on Friday.
Daniel didn't swim in the sea.

title: When? Time words for the past
summary: Time words such as أَمْسِ (yesterday), الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِي (last week) and مُنْذُ (ago) tell when something happened.
formula: past verb + time word: زُرْتُ سَامِي الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِي · مُنْذُ + time = ago
explanation: A time phrase used without a preposition takes the -a ending: الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِي (last week), يَوْمَ السَّبْت (on Saturday), صَبَاحًا (in the morning), مَسَاءً (in the evening). You can also say it with فِي: فِي الْأُسْبُوعِ الْمَاضِي. الْمَاضِي (past, last) agrees with its noun: الشَّهْرَ الْمَاضِي (last month) but السَّنَةَ الْمَاضِيَة (last year). مُنْذُ + a time means 'ago' with a past verb: وَصَلْتُ مُنْذُ أُسْبُوع (I arrived a week ago).

examples.en: I cleaned my flat last week.
I arrived in Cairo a month ago.

title: كَانَ: was, were
summary: كَانَ (was) puts a description in the past, and the describing word takes the -an ending: كَانَ الْجَوُّ لَطِيفًا (the weather was pleasant).
formula: كَانَ / كَانَتْ + subject + description with -an: كَانَتِ الرِّحْلَةُ مُمْتِعَةً
explanation: In the present Arabic needs no word for 'is': الْجَوُّ لَطِيف (the weather is pleasant). In the past you add كَانَ, and the description changes its ending to -an (-a with al-): كَانَ الْجَوُّ لَطِيفًا. كَانَ is a hollow verb: before the endings -tu, -ta, -nā its long ā shortens and the stem becomes kun-: كُنْتُ (I was), كُنَّا (we were). كَانَ هُنَاكَ means 'there was': كَانَ هُنَاكَ مَطْعَم صَغِير (there was a small restaurant).

examples.en: The holiday was great fun.
I was in Lebanon in the summer.

title: Before and after: قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ
summary: قَبْلَ (before) and بَعْدَ (after) come before a noun, a pronoun ending, or أَنْ + a verb.
formula: قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ + noun (-i) · + pronoun (بَعْدَهُ) · بَعْدَ أَنْ + past verb
explanation: قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ work like the first word of a possessive phrase, so the noun after them takes the -i ending: قَبْلَ الْعَشَاءِ (before dinner), بَعْدَ الدَّرْسِ (after the lesson). They also take pronoun endings: بَعْدَهُ (after it). Before a whole action add أَنْ (that): بَعْدَ أَنْ أَكَلْنَا (after we ate). بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ (after that) and ثُمَّ (then) link the steps of a story. With a length of time, قَبْلَ means 'ago', like مُنْذُ: قَبْلَ يَوْمَيْنِ (two days ago).

examples.en: I washed my hands before dinner.

examples.ar: بَعْدَ أَنْ أَكَلْنَا، لَعِبَ عُمَر بِالْكُرَة.
examples.en: After we ate, Omar played with the ball.

title: لَمْ: did not (the written standard)
summary: لَمْ + the present form of the verb, with a sukūn at the end, means 'did not': لَمْ أَذْهَبْ (I didn't go).
formula: لَمْ + present verb; final -u → sukūn: أَذْهَبُ → لَمْ أَذْهَبْ · -ūna → -ū: يَذْهَبُونَ → لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا
explanation: لَمْ is the standard way to say 'didn't' in writing and in careful speech. It surprises learners twice. First, it takes the present form, not the past: لَمْ أَذْهَبْ, never لَمْ ذَهَبْتُ. Second, the verb changes its ending: the final -u becomes a sukūn (أَكْتُبُ → لَمْ أَكْتُبْ), and the endings -ūna and -īna lose their n (تَذْهَبِينَ → لَمْ تَذْهَبِي). It means the same as مَا + past (day 37), which is more relaxed. لَمْ … بَعْدُ means 'not yet': لَمْ أَكْتُبْهَا بَعْدُ (I haven't written them yet).

examples.en: I didn't go to school yesterday.
I haven't written the homework yet.

title: What hurts: يُؤْلِمُنِي and تُؤْلِمُنِي
summary: Arabic says 'it hurts me': the verb comes first, and it matches the body part: يُؤْلِمُنِي for a masculine part, تُؤْلِمُنِي for a feminine one.
formula: يُؤْلِمُنِي + masculine part · تُؤْلِمُنِي + feminine part
explanation: يُؤْلِمُنِي رَأْسِي is 'my head hurts me'. The body part is the subject, so the verb agrees with it. Most body parts are masculine, but the parts that come in pairs, يَد (hand), رِجْل (leg, foot), عَيْن (eye) and أُذُن (ear), are feminine without ة, so they take تُؤْلِمُنِي. Change the ending of the verb for other people: يُؤْلِمُكَ (it hurts you, to a man), يُؤْلِمُهُ (it hurts him). You can also put the body part first: رَأْسِي يُؤْلِمُنِي.

examples.en: My back hurts.
My eye hurts.

title: Giving orders: the imperative
summary: To give an order, take the 'you' form of the present, drop the ta- at the front and the vowel at the end: تَفْتَحُ (you open) → اِفْتَحْ (open!).
formula: تَفْتَحُ → اِفْتَحْ (to a man) · اِفْتَحِي (to a woman) · اِفْتَحُوا (to a group)
explanation: Start from the 'you' form of the present tense: تَفْتَحُ (you open). Drop the ta-. If the word now starts with two consonants (fta-), add a helping vowel in front: اِ (i) when the middle vowel is a or i, as in اِفْتَحْ and اِجْلِسْ, and اُ (u) when it is u, as in اُرْكُضْ (run!). The end is sukūn for a man, ـِي for a woman and ـُوا for a group. If the word already starts with consonant + vowel, no helper is needed: تَتَنَفَّسُ → تَنَفَّسْ (breathe!). A few common verbs are short and irregular: خُذْ (take!), كُلْ (eat!), نَمْ (sleep!).

examples.en: Open your mouth, please. (to a man)
Sit here, please. (to a woman)

title: I want to…: أَنْ + the present
summary: To join a verb like 'want' or 'can' to a second verb, put أَنْ (an, 'that') between them. The second verb keeps its person and ends in -a.
formula: أُرِيدُ + أَنْ + أَشْتَرِيَ (present tense, ending -a)
explanation: English says 'I want to buy'; Arabic says 'I want that I buy': أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشْتَرِيَ. Both verbs show the person: تُرِيدُ أَنْ تَجْلِسَ (you want to sit). After أَنْ the present tense takes the subjunctive ending: the last vowel -u becomes -a, so أَشْرَبُ (I drink) becomes أَنْ أَشْرَبَ (to drink). Endings in -na drop it: tashrabīna (you drink, to a woman) becomes an tashrabī. In everyday speech the vowel endings are often not heard, but أَنْ itself is needed in standard Arabic.

أَنْ + second verb
English
rows: I want to buy some medicine
I don't want to eat anything

examples.en: I want to buy some tissues.
Do you want to sit down? (to a man)

title: How I feel: adjectives that agree
summary: Say how you feel with أَنَا + an adjective. The adjective agrees with the person: add ة for a woman; a few adjectives in -ān change to -ā.
formula: أَنَا + adjective (+ ة for a woman) · أَشْعُرُ بِـ + noun
explanation: No verb 'to be' is needed: أَنَا مُتْعَب (I am tired, said by a man), أَنَا مُتْعَبَة (said by a woman). Most adjectives simply add ة. Adjectives on the pattern faʿlān, like عَطْشَان (thirsty) and غَضْبَان (angry), have a feminine in -ā in standard Arabic: عَطْشَى, غَضْبَى (everyday speech often says ʿaṭshāna). With the verb أَشْعُرُ (I feel) use بِـ and a noun, أَشْعُرُ بِالْمَلَل (I feel bored, literally 'I feel boredom'), or a whole sentence: أَشْعُرُ أَنَّنِي أَحْسَن (I feel better).

examples.en: I am very happy. (a woman)
Are you thirsty? (to a man)

title: Don't…!: لَا + the present without -u
summary: To tell someone not to do something, keep the 'you' form of the present, put لَا in front and end it like an order: لَا تَشْرَبْ (don't drink!).
formula: لَا تَشْرَبْ (to a man) · لَا تَشْرَبِي (to a woman) · لَا تَشْرَبُوا (to a group)
explanation: Unlike the positive order, the ta- stays: تَشْرَبُ (you drink) → لَا تَشْرَبْ (don't drink!). The ending changes as in the imperative: sukūn for a man, ـِي for a woman and ـُوا for a group. Before الـ the sukūn becomes i so the words join: لَا تَشْرَبِ الْقَهْوَة (don't drink the coffee). Verbs that end in a long vowel shorten it: تَنْسَى (you forget) → لَا تَنْسَ (don't forget!), and to a woman لَا تَنْسَيْ. Be careful: لَا تَشْرَبُ with -u is a statement, 'you don't drink'.

examples.en: Don't forget the medicine! (to a man)
Don't drink coffee now. (to a woman)

title: Must: لَازِم and يَجِبُ + أَنْ
summary: To say 'must' or 'have to', use لَازِم (necessary) or يَجِبُ (it is necessary) + أَنْ + the present tense ending in -a.
formula: لَازِم / يَجِبُ + أَنْ + present (ending -a)
explanation: لَازِم and يَجِبُ never change: the person is shown on the second verb. لَازِم أَنْ أَرْتَاحَ (I must rest), لَازِم أَنْ تَرْتَاحَ (you must rest), يَجِبُ أَنْ يَنَامَ (he must sleep). لَازِم is very common when people speak; يَجِبُ is a little more formal and common in writing. To ask 'do I have to…?' put هَلْ in front: هَلْ يَجِبُ أَنْ آخُذَ الدَّوَاء؟ To say 'it is not necessary', use لَيْسَ ضَرُورِيًّا.

head: Arabic
English
rows: you must go to bed early
do I have to take the medicine?

examples.en: You must rest today and tomorrow. (to a man)
I must go to bed early.

title: The future: سَـ and سَوْفَ
summary: To talk about the future, put سَـ (sa-) or سَوْفَ (sawfa) in front of a present-tense verb: أَزُورُ (I visit) → سَأَزُورُ (I will visit).
formula: سَـ + present verb, written as one word: سَأَزُورُ · سَوْفَ + present verb, two words: سَوْفَ أَزُورُ
explanation: Arabic has no separate future tense. Take the present tense you already know and put سَـ in front of it, written joined to the verb: أَنَامُ (I sleep) → سَأَنَامُ (I will sleep), نَذْهَبُ (we go) → سَنَذْهَبُ (we will go). The person prefix and ending stay exactly the same. سَوْفَ means the same thing but is a separate word: سَوْفَ أَتَّصِلُ (I will call). The future of كَانَ is سَيَكُونُ (he, it will be), and like كَانَ it puts the describing word in the -an form: سَأَكُونُ مَشْغُولًا (I will be busy). To ask about plans, say مَاذَا سَتَفْعَلُ غَدًا؟ (what will you do tomorrow?). Never put سَـ or سَوْفَ in front of a past verb. The negative ('I won't') uses a different word, which comes on day 51.

examples.en: I will visit the pyramids the day after tomorrow.
What will you do tomorrow? (to a man)
I will call my sister in the evening.

title: I won't: لَنْ + the present
summary: To say 'won't', put لَنْ in front of a present verb and end the verb in -a: سَأَنَامُ (I will sleep) → لَنْ أَنَامَ (I won't sleep).
formula: لَنْ + present verb ending in -a: لَنْ أَنَامَ · لَنْ نَرْكَبَ · لَنْ تَأْتِيَ
explanation: The future has its own negative word. Do not say لَا سَأَنَامُ: drop سَـ and put لَنْ in front of the present verb instead. After لَنْ the verb takes the same -a ending as after أَنْ: أَنَامُ → لَنْ أَنَامَ (I won't sleep), سَتَأْتِي → لَنْ تَأْتِيَ (she won't come). A verb that ends in a long ā does not change: لَنْ أَنْسَى (I won't forget). For two people the -ni ending drops: لَنْ يَرْكَبَا (they two won't take). With أَبَدًا it means 'never': لَنْ أُسَافِرَ أَبَدًا (I will never travel). Remember the three negatives: لَا for the present, لَمْ for the past and لَنْ for the future.

head: Future
Won't
English
rows: we won't take, we won't ride

examples.en: I won't go to bed late tonight.

examples.ar: لَيْلَى لَنْ تَأْتِيَ مَعَنَا فِي الصَّبَاح.
examples.en: Layla won't come with us in the morning.

title: In order to: لِـ + the present
summary: To say why you do something, put لِـ (li-) in front of a present verb ending in -a: سَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوق لِأَشْتَرِيَ هَدِيَّة (I'll go to the market to buy a present).
formula: action + لِـ + present verb ending in -a: لِأَشْتَرِيَ · لِنَشْتَرِيَ · لِتَصْنَعَ
explanation: English uses 'to' for a purpose: 'I went out to buy bread'. Arabic uses لِـ (li-, 'for, so that'), written joined to the verb. As after أَنْ, the verb keeps its person and ends in -a: أَشْتَرِي (I buy) → لِأَشْتَرِيَ (to buy, so that I buy), نَشْتَرِي (we buy) → لِنَشْتَرِيَ (so that we buy). The person is the one who does the second action: سَتَأْتِي أُمِّي لِتَصْنَعَ الْكَعْكَة (my mother will come to make the cake). Don't mix it up with أَنْ: أَنْ follows verbs such as أُرِيدُ (I want) and أَسْتَطِيعُ (I can), while لِـ gives the reason for an action.

head: Action
لِـ + verb
English
rows: I'll go to the market to buy a present
we'll go to Khan el-Khalili to buy a present
my mother will come to make the cake
I've come to invite you (to a man)

examples.en: My mother is coming from Beirut to make the cake.

title: Talking about the weather
summary: Describe the weather with الْجَوّ (the weather) + an adjective: الْجَوّ حَارّ (it's hot). Rain has its own verb, تُمْطِرُ (it rains), and the temperature is دَرَجَةُ الْحَرَارَة + a number.
formula: الْجَوّ + adjective: الْجَوّ بَارِد · تُمْطِرُ / أَمْطَرَتْ / سَتُمْطِرُ · دَرَجَةُ الْحَرَارَة + number
explanation: English says 'it is hot', with an empty 'it'. Arabic names the weather instead: الْجَوّ حَارّ (the weather is hot), الْجَوّ غَائِم (it's cloudy). For rain there is a verb, used in the feminine because 'the sky' is understood: تُمْطِرُ (it rains, it's raining), أَمْطَرَتْ (it rained), سَتُمْطِرُ (it will rain). For snow say يَنْزِلُ الثَّلْج (snow falls). For wind use هُنَاكَ: هُنَاكَ رِيَاح قَوِيَّة (it's very windy). To ask, say كَيْفَ الطَّقْس؟ (what's the weather like?). In the past and the future, كَانَ and سَيَكُونُ put the adjective in the -an form: كَانَ الْجَوّ بَارِدًا (it was cold), سَيَكُونُ الْجَوّ بَارِدًا (it will be cold).

examples.en: It's hot and sunny in Cairo.
It will rain in Amman tomorrow.

title: يَكُونُ: is usually, will be
summary: يَكُونُ is the present form of كَانَ. Use it for what is usually true (فِي الصَّيْف يَكُونُ الْجَوّ حَارًّا, in summer the weather is hot) and, with سَـ, for the future: سَيَكُونُ (it will be).
formula: (سَـ) يَكُونُ / تَكُونُ + subject + describing word with -an: يَكُونُ الْجَوّ حَارًّا
explanation: In the present, Arabic usually needs no verb 'to be': الْجَوّ حَارّ (the weather is hot). But كَانَ has a present form, يَكُونُ, and it is used in two places. First, for what is usually or always true, often with a time phrase: فِي الشِّتَاء يَكُونُ الْجَوّ بَارِدًا (in winter the weather is cold). Second, for the future, with سَـ: سَيَكُونُ الْجَوّ حَارًّا (it will be hot), سَأَكُونُ مَشْغُولًا (I will be busy). Like كَانَ, it changes the describing word to the -an form: حَارّ → حَارًّا. With a feminine subject, and with plurals of things, use تَكُونُ: تَكُونُ الْحَرَارَة أَرْبَعِينَ دَرَجَةً (the temperature is forty degrees).

head: Person
Is (usually)
Will be
English
rows: you are / you will be (to a man)

examples.en: In summer the weather is hot.
Winter will be cold in Amman.

title: Next week, next month: الْقَادِم, and the months
summary: For the future, use الْقَادِم (next, coming) where you used الْمَاضِي (last) for the past: الشَّهْرَ الْقَادِمَ (next month), السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ (next year). For a month, use فِي: فِي مَارِس (in March).
formula: الشَّهْرَ الْقَادِمَ · السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ · فِي (شَهْرِ) + month: فِي شَهْرِ مَارِس
explanation: On day 38 you met الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِي (last week). Its partner for the future is الْقَادِم (coming, next): الشَّهْرَ الْقَادِمَ (next month). Like any adjective it agrees with its noun, so a feminine noun takes ة: السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ (next year), الشُّهُور الْقَادِمَة (the coming months). Used without a preposition, the time phrase takes the -a ending, just like الشَّهْرَ الْمَاضِي. For a month use فِي, with or without the word شَهْر: فِي دِيسَمْبِر or فِي شَهْرِ دِيسَمْبِر (in December). The month names below are the ones used in Egypt; Lebanon, Syria and Jordan use older names.

examples.en: We'll travel to Amman next month.
Next year I'll visit Lebanon.

title: Dates: the fifth of November
summary: Say a date with an ordinal, then مِنْ (of), then the month: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر (the fifth of November). To ask, say مَا تَارِيخُ الْيَوْم؟ (what's the date today?).
formula: الـ + ordinal (masculine) + مِنْ + month: السَّابِعُ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر · on a date: فِي السَّابِعِ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر
explanation: A date is 'the Nth day of the month'. Use the ordinal with الـ, in the masculine because يَوْم (day) is masculine, then مِنْ (of, from), then the month: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر. To say 'on' a date, use فِي: فِي السَّابِعِ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر (on the seventh of November). You can put the weekday first: يَوْمَ الْأَحَد، التَّاسِعِ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر. Don't mix it up with the time: the hour is feminine, so السَّاعَة السَّابِعَة is seven o'clock, while السَّابِعُ مِنْ نُوفَمْبِر is a date. From the 11th on, people usually just read the number before the month. Dates are written day first, then month: ٧/١١ is the seventh of November.

examples.en: Today is the fifth of November.
The party is on the seventh of November.

title: Is it possible? مُمْكِن
summary: To ask politely whether you may do something, say هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِن أَنْ…؟ (is it possible to…?) + a present verb ending in -a. The answer is مُمْكِن (possible) or غَيْرُ مُمْكِن (not possible).
formula: هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِن + أَنْ + present (ending -a)؟
explanation: مُمْكِن means 'possible', and مِنَ الْمُمْكِن (literally 'of the possible') means 'it is possible'. Put هَلْ in front and you have the most useful polite question for a traveller: هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِن أَنْ أَجْلِسَ بِجَانِبِ النَّافِذَة؟ (could I sit by the window?). The verb after أَنْ shows who does the action and ends in -a: أَنْ آخُذَ (that I take), أَنْ نَشْرَبَ (that we drink), أَنْ تُسَاعِدَنِي (that you help me). In everyday speech the question is often shortened to مُمْكِن أَنْ…؟ or just مُمْكِن؟ with a rising voice. Answer نَعَم، مُمْكِن (yes, that's possible) or لِلْأَسَف، هٰذَا غَيْرُ مُمْكِن (unfortunately, that isn't possible).

English

examples.en: May I see the passport?

title: Polite requests: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ, هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ…؟, أَرْجُو أَنْ…
summary: Make a request polite in three ways: add لَوْ سَمَحْتَ or مِنْ فَضْلِكَ, ask هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ…؟ (can you…?), or begin with أَرْجُو أَنْ… (I would ask you to…).
formula: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ + request · هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ + verb (-a)؟ · أَرْجُو أَنْ + verb (-a)
explanation: An order such as تَعَالَ (come!) is fine between friends, but with strangers Arabic speakers soften their requests. (1) Add لَوْ سَمَحْتَ ('if you allow') or مِنْ فَضْلِكَ ('please') before or after the request. Both change with the person: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ to a man, لَوْ سَمَحْتِ to a woman, لَوْ سَمَحْتُمْ to a group. لَوْ سَمَحْتَ is also how you get someone's attention: 'excuse me'. (2) Ask whether the person can do it: هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ تُوقِظَنَا؟ (could you wake us?). (3) Begin with أَرْجُو أَنْ… (literally 'I hope that you…'), a polite and slightly formal 'please': أَرْجُو أَنْ تَطْلُبَ لَنَا تَاكْسِي (please order a taxi for us). After أَنْ the verb ends in -a, as usual. When you hand something over, say تَفَضَّلْ (here you are), or تَفَضَّلِي to a woman.

head: Arabic
English
Use
rows: Excuse me, where is the lift?
Excuse me, where is the lift?
Please order a taxi for us.
Here you are, this is my passport.

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the lift?

examples.en: Could you order us a taxi?

title: Hollow verbs: زَارَ, زُرْتُ, يَزُورُ
summary: Some verbs have a long vowel in the middle: زَارَ (he visited), يَزُورُ (he visits). In the past the long ā becomes short before endings like -tu, -ta and -nā: زُرْتُ (I visited), نِمْتُ (I slept).
formula: he: زَارَ (long ā) → I: زُرْتُ (short) · present: يَزُورُ (long ū, ī or ā)
explanation: In verbs like قَالَ (said), زَارَ (visited), كَانَ (was), عَادَ (returned), نَامَ (slept) and بَاعَ (sold), the middle of the word is a long vowel, not a consonant, so they are called 'hollow'. With he, she and they the past keeps the long ā: زَارَ، زَارَتْ، زَارُوا. With I, you and we the ending begins with a consonant, and the long vowel becomes short: زُرْتُ (I visited), قُلْتُ (I said), كُنَّا (we were), عُدْتُ (I returned); verbs like نَامَ and بَاعَ take i instead: نِمْتُ (I slept), بِعْتُ (I sold). The present tense shows the verb's vowel: يَزُورُ and يَقُولُ have ū, يَبِيعُ has ī, يَنَامُ has ā. When the verb ends in a sukūn, the vowel is short again: after لَمْ you say لَمْ نَزُرْهَا (we didn't visit it). Orders to a group keep the long vowel: زُورُوا (visit!), نَامُوا (sleep!).

examples.en: Have you visited Petra before?
We have never visited it.

title: Help me! Object endings on verbs
summary: The endings you know from nouns also go on verbs, where they mean me, you, him, her, it, us and them. Only 'me' is different: on a verb it is ـنِي (-nī), not ـِي.
formula: verb + ـنِي · ـكَ · ـكِ · ـهُ · ـهَا · ـنَا · ـكُمْ · ـهُمْ
explanation: An object pronoun ('me', 'him', 'it'…) is joined to the end of the verb: أُسَاعِدُكَ (I help you), رَأَيْتُكَ (I saw you), سَأَلْنَاهُ (we asked him). The endings are the same as on nouns (غُرْفَتُكَ, غُرْفَتُهَا), except 'me': غُرْفَتِي is 'my room', but سَاعِدْنِي is 'help me!' and تُسَاعِدَنِي is '(that) you help me'. Never use أَنَا as an object. A thing is 'it' with ـهُ for a masculine word and ـهَا for a feminine word: the wallet, مِحْفَظَة, is feminine, so 'I found it' is وَجَدْتُهَا. After أَنْ the verb still ends in -a in front of the ending: أَنْ تُسَاعِدَنِي (to help me), أَنْ تَضَعَهَا (to put it).

examples.en: Can you help me?
I found it on the table.

title: Bigger than: أَكْبَرُ مِنْ
summary: To compare, put the three root letters of an adjective into the pattern a-CCaC and add مِنْ (than): كَبِير (big) → أَكْبَرُ مِنْ (bigger than). The form is the same for masculine and feminine.
formula: a-CCaC + مِنْ:  كَبِير → أَكْبَرُ مِنْ
explanation: Take the three root letters of the adjective and put them into the pattern a-CCaC: كَبِير (big) → أَكْبَر (bigger), صَغِير (small) → أَصْغَر (smaller), رَخِيص (cheap) → أَرْخَص (cheaper), بَارِد (cold) → أَبْرَد (colder). 'Than' is مِنْ: الْقَاهِرَة أَكْبَرُ مِنْ عَمَّان (Cairo is bigger than Amman). The comparative never changes, whatever it describes: الْمَدِينَة أَكْبَرُ (the city is bigger), الْبَيْت أَكْبَرُ (the house is bigger), الْأَسْعَار أَرْخَصُ (the prices are cheaper). Adjectives ending in a weak letter end in -ā: غَالٍ (expensive) → أَغْلَى, قَوِيّ (strong) → أَقْوَى. Adjectives with a doubled letter keep it together: قَلِيل (few) → أَقَلّ (fewer, less). 'Much bigger' is أَكْبَرُ بِكَثِير. Some adjectives, like مُزْدَحِم (crowded), have no a-CCaC form; then say أَكْثَرُ (more) + a noun ending in -an: أَكْثَرُ ازْدِحَامًا (more crowded).

examples.en: Cairo is bigger than Amman.
The weather here is colder than in Cairo.

title: The biggest: أَكْبَرُ مَدِينَة
summary: The a-CCaC form also means 'the most'. Put it in front of a noun without الـ: أَكْبَرُ مَدِينَة (the biggest city). Before a plural with الـ it means 'the …-est of': مِنْ أَكْبَرِ الْمَسَارِح (one of the biggest theatres).
formula: a-CCaC + noun (no الـ) = the …-est · مِنْ + a-CCaC + plural with الـ = one of the …-est
explanation: You already know أَكْبَرُ مِنْ (bigger than). Without مِنْ, and placed in front of a noun, the same word means 'the biggest': عَمَّان أَكْبَرُ مَدِينَة فِي الْأُرْدُنّ (Amman is the biggest city in Jordan). The noun after it is singular and has no الـ, and the superlative itself takes no الـ either. The form does not change for feminine nouns: أَجْمَلُ صُورَة (the most beautiful photo), أَفْضَلُ رِحْلَة (the best trip). To say 'one of the most…', use مِنْ + the superlative + a plural with الـ: مِنْ أَعْلَى الْجِبَال (one of the highest hills), مِنْ أَكْبَرِ الْمَسَارِح (one of the biggest theatres). أَفْضَلُ (better, best) works the same way: أَفْضَلُ مَكَان (the best place).

English

الْبَحْر الْمَيِّت أَخْفَضُ مَكَان فِي الْعَالَم.
The Dead Sea is the lowest place in the world.
This is the best trip of my life.

It is one of the biggest theatres in Jordan.

examples.en: Amman is the biggest city in Jordan.
Petra is the most famous place in Jordan.

title: Can: يُمْكِنُ + a person ending + أَنْ
summary: To say 'can', use يُمْكِنُ (it is possible) with a person ending, then أَنْ and a present verb ending in -a: يُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَكْتُبَ (I can write).
formula: يُمْكِنُنِي / يُمْكِنُكَ / يُمْكِنُكِ / يُمْكِنُهُ / يُمْكِنُنَا + أَنْ + present (ending -a)
explanation: يُمْكِنُ never changes. The person who can is an ending on it, as on a noun: يُمْكِنُنِي (I can, literally 'it is possible for me'), يُمْكِنُكَ (you can, to a man), يُمْكِنُهُ (he can). The second verb follows أَنْ and has its own person: يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تَسْأَلَنِي (you can ask me). To ask politely, put هَلْ in front: هَلْ يُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَسْتَعْمِلَ الْحَاسُوب؟ (Can I use the computer?). Without an ending it means 'it is possible' or 'could': هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تَتَّصِلَ بِي؟ (Could you call me?). For 'cannot' put لَا in front: لَا يُمْكِنُنِي.

head: Arabic
English
rows: you can read it (to a woman)

examples.ar: هَلْ يُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَسْتَعْمِلَ هٰذَا الْحَاسُوب؟
examples.en: Can I use this computer?
You can write the report tomorrow. (to a man)

title: The verbal noun (maṣdar): reading, writing, studying
summary: Every verb has a noun that names the action: قَرَأَ (read) → قِرَاءَة (reading). Use it like any noun: أُحِبُّ الْقِرَاءَة (I love reading).
formula: verb → verbal noun · أُحِبُّ + الْمَصْدَر = أُحِبُّ أَنْ + verb
explanation: The maṣdar is the '-ing' word of English: الْقِرَاءَة (reading), الْكِتَابَة (writing), الدِّرَاسَة (studying). For simple (Form I) verbs the shape has to be learnt with each verb: قَرَأَ → قِرَاءَة, كَتَبَ → كِتَابَة, دَرَسَ → دِرَاسَة, عَمِلَ → عَمَل. For the longer verb patterns it is regular: عَلَّمَ → تَعْلِيم, تَعَلَّمَ → تَعَلُّم, اِجْتَمَعَ → اِجْتِمَاع. A maṣdar can be the subject (الْقِرَاءَة مُهِمَّة, reading is important), the object (أُحِبُّ الْقِرَاءَة) or the first word of an iḍāfa: دِرَاسَةُ الْعَرَبِيَّة (the study of Arabic, studying Arabic). أُحِبُّ الْقِرَاءَة and أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَقْرَأَ mean the same.

examples.en: I love reading and writing.
Studying Arabic is fun.

title: The active participle: going, travelling, sure
summary: The active participle describes what someone is doing now or is about to do: أَنَا ذَاهِب إِلَى الْمَكْتَب (I'm going to the office). It agrees like an adjective.
formula: Form I: فَاعِل (ذَاهِب) · other forms: مُـ + present stem with -i- (مُسَافِر)
explanation: For simple verbs the pattern is fāʿil: ذَهَبَ → ذَاهِب (going), حَضَرَ → حَاضِر (present). When the middle root letter is weak, a hamza takes its place: عَادَ → عَائِد (coming back), غَابَ → غَائِب (away). For the other verb patterns take the present, swap the first syllable for مُـ and make the last vowel i: يُسَافِرُ → مُسَافِر (travelling), يَتَأَكَّدُ → مُتَأَكِّد (sure), يَسْتَعِدُّ → مُسْتَعِدّ (ready). It needs no verb 'to be' and agrees with the person: هُوَ مُسَافِر, هِيَ مُسَافِرَة. Many participles are also words for people: مُدَرِّس (teacher, 'one who teaches'), مُتَرْجِم (translator).

examples.en: I'm going to the office.
The manager is travelling today.

title: Writing an email: the fixed phrases
summary: Formal Arabic emails and letters follow a fixed order: a title for the person, a greeting, the subject, then a closing phrase.
formula: حَضْرَةَ … الْمُحْتَرَم، → تَحِيَّة طَيِّبَة وَبَعْدُ، → the subject → مَعَ أَطْيَبِ التَّحِيَّات، + name
explanation: To someone you don't know well, start with حَضْرَةَ (a title of respect) + the person + الْمُحْتَرَم (the respected), or الْمُحْتَرَمَة for a woman. To a friend or a close colleague write عَزِيزِي (dear, to a man) or عَزِيزَتِي (to a woman). Then comes the greeting تَحِيَّة طَيِّبَة وَبَعْدُ, literally 'a good greeting, and after that', which tells the reader that the subject follows. Useful sentences: أَرْجُو أَنْ تَكُونَ بِخَيْر (I hope you are well), مُرْفَق مَعَ هٰذِهِ الرِّسَالَة… (attached to this message is…), فِي انْتِظَارِ رَدِّكُمْ (I look forward to your reply). End with مَعَ أَطْيَبِ التَّحِيَّات (with best regards) or مَعَ الشُّكْر (with thanks), and your name.

Arabic
English

title: Verb patterns: one root, many verbs
summary: Arabic builds verbs from a root of three letters and a pattern. The root gives the idea (d-r-s: study); the pattern adds a meaning: دَرَسَ (studied), دَرَّسَ (taught).
formula: root (ف ع ل) + pattern: فَعَلَ · فَعَّلَ · فَاعَلَ · أَفْعَلَ · تَفَعَّلَ · اِفْتَعَلَ · اِسْتَفْعَلَ
explanation: Grammar books show the patterns with the model root ف ع ل (do). The simple verb is Form I, فَعَلَ: دَرَسَ, كَتَبَ. Form II, فَعَّلَ, doubles the middle letter and often means 'make someone do it': دَرَّسَ (taught), عَلَّمَ (taught). Form III, فَاعَلَ, adds ā and often means doing something with or to someone: سَاعَدَ (helped), سَافَرَ (travelled). Form IV, أَفْعَلَ: أَرْسَلَ (sent). Form V, تَفَعَّلَ, is ta- + Form II, often 'do it to yourself': تَعَلَّمَ (learnt), تَكَلَّمَ (spoke). Form VIII, اِفْتَعَلَ, puts t after the first letter: اِجْتَمَعَ (met), اِنْتَظَرَ (waited). Form X, اِسْتَفْعَلَ: اِسْتَعْمَلَ (used). Each pattern also has a fixed present: يُدَرِّسُ, يُسَاعِدُ, يُرْسِلُ, يَتَعَلَّمُ, يَجْتَمِعُ, يَسْتَعْمِلُ. Learn to hear the pattern, and you can guess new words.

examples.en: Mr Karim teaches Arabic.
We meet at the office every morning.
